attributes.nuance_translation: An expression that groups the previous information, and then describes it further.

attributes.body:
In Japanese, のは and のが behave in a very similar way to the words 'that' and 'which' in English. This means that they perform a task called nominalization. Nominalization is when a phrase is treated in the same way as a single noun.

Rather than a single noun, we can see from these examples that the phrases 沢山（たくさん）食（た）べるのは and バスに乗（の）るのが are behaving in the same way that a single noun would. In English, this can either mean 'that which', or 'the one who/that'.

This construction can be used after verbs in any tense, except for the polite ます or ません, which are only used at the end of a sentence, or certain clauses.

Caution

の cannot be used as a substitute for こと in set expressions like ことができる, or ことがある. It also may not be followed by だ, である, or です, as this would become the explanatory ～んです, or のです in that case.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: Difference between の and こと nominalizers
The Nominalizers の and こと

attributes.body: The particle の often shows possession, like the English ''s' (e.g., ケンジの本 means 'Kenji's book'). It can also connect two nouns, as in 日本人の学生 ('a student who is Japanese'). In contrast, は marks the topic of the sentence. Unlike の, it doesn't show possession — it introduces what the rest of the sentence will describe or explain.

first_relatable.title: の
first_relatable.meaning: Verb nominalizer, The one who..., That which...

attributes.body: In the phrase AのB, の indicates a relationship between A and B, either possession (e.g., ジョンの本 = 'John's book') or description (e.g., 日本人の学生 = 'A Japanese student'). Particle + の is a variation where a phrase with a particle describes another noun (e.g., 先生からの手紙 = 'A letter from the teacher'). Note that particles like に, も, は, が, and を are typically not used in this construction.

second_relatable.title: の
second_relatable.meaning: Verb nominalizer, The one who..., That which...

attributes.body: The particle の connects nouns to indicate possession or description. For example, 私の本 means 'my book.' When used with the pronoun の (meaning 'one'), the second の is dropped. For instance, to say 'It's mine,' you would say 私のです, not 私ののです.

second_relatable.title: の
second_relatable.meaning: Verb nominalizer, The one who..., That which...

attributes.body: の shows possession, like the English 's' (e.g., ケンジの本 = 'Kenji's book'). が marks the subject of a clause, often the doer of an action or the one with a certain trait. In modifying phrases, の and が are sometimes interchangeable without changing the meaning—for example, 先生が書いた本 and 先生の書いた本 both mean 'the book the teacher wrote.'

first_relatable.title: の
first_relatable.meaning: Verb nominalizer, The one who..., That which...

attributes.body: Both of these patterns use の to turn a phrase into a noun. For example, the verb 走る ('to run') becomes 走るのが好き ('I like running') because the subject marker が must follow a noun. The Adjective + の(は) pattern works similarly, turning adjectives into noun phrases (e.g., 赤い ('red') becomes 赤いのはきれいです ('The red one is pretty')).

first_relatable.title: の
first_relatable.meaning: Verb nominalizer, The one who..., That which...

attributes.body: Both こと and の turn verbs or adjectives into noun phrases. こと is used for intangible or conceptual ideas, while の is used for more tangible or physical concepts. For example, 走るのが好きです and 走ることが好きです both mean 'I like running,' with の feeling more physical and こと more conceptual. However, they aren't interchangeable in set phrases like ことができる or ことがある.
